# 2 Maccabees Chapter 13 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_013_page_001.jpg

---

**13:1** In the one hundred forty-ninth year, word came to Judas and his men that Antiochus Eupator was advancing against Judea with a great multitude,

**13:2** and with him Lysias, his guardian and administrator of affairs of state, each commanding a Greek force of a hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred scythed chariots.

**13:3** Menelaus joined them as well, urging on Antiochus with a great show of enthusiasm — not for the welfare of his country, but in the hope of being confirmed in office.

**13:4** But the King of kings stirred up Antiochus's anger against this villain. And when Lysias informed him that Menelaus was the cause of all the troubles, the king ordered him to be taken to Beroea and there put to death by the method customary in that place.

**13:5** For there is a tower there, fifty cubits high, filled with ashes, equipped on all sides with a rim that slopes precipitously inward toward the ashes.

**13:6** Into this, anyone guilty of sacrilege or notorious for other crimes is thrust to destruction.

**13:7** By such a fate Menelaus the lawbreaker met his end — not even receiving burial in the earth;

**13:8** and justly so, since he had committed many sins against the altar whose fire and ashes were holy, he received his death in ashes.

**13:9** The king came on, his mind full of savage intent, determined to make the Jews suffer far worse than they had endured under his father.

**13:10** When Judas learned of this, he ordered the people to call upon the Lord day and night — now above all, to come to the aid of those who were about to be robbed of their law, their homeland, and the holy temple,

**13:11** and not to let the people who had only just begun to breathe again fall into the hands of the blasphemous Gentiles.

**13:12** When all had done this together — lying prostrate on their faces for three days, weeping and fasting without ceasing, and beseeching the merciful Lord — Judas urged them to readiness and commanded them to stand by.

**13:13** In private consultation with the elders, he resolved to march out and determine the issue by the help of God before the king's army could enter Judea and take the city.

**13:14** Entrusting the outcome to the Creator of the world, and exhorting his men to fight nobly to the death for the law, the temple, the city, the fatherland, and the ancestral way of life, he pitched camp near Modein.

**13:15** Giving his men the watchword "Victory comes from God," he led the finest young men he had in a night assault on the royal tent and killed some two thousand men in the camp, and ran through the lead elephant together with its mahout.

**13:16** In the end they filled the whole camp with terror and confusion and withdrew, having triumphed.

**13:17** This was accomplished just as dawn was breaking, because the Lord's protection had shielded him.

**13:18** The king, having had a taste of the daring of the Jews, tried to take their positions by stratagem.

**13:19** He marched against Beth-zur, a strong Jewish fortress, but was driven back, failed, and lost men.

**13:20** Maccabeus sent in to those inside whatever was needed.

**13:21** But Rhodocus, a man from the Jewish ranks, disclosed secret information to the enemy. He was tracked down, arrested, and imprisoned.

**13:22** The king opened negotiations again with those in Beth-zur, gave his right hand as pledge, received theirs, and withdrew.

**13:23** He attacked Judas and was repulsed. Then word reached him that Philip, whom he had left in charge at Antioch, had revolted. Dismayed, he proposed terms to the Jews, agreed to all just conditions, swore oaths, and departed. He sacrificed to the Lord and honored the temple, and was generous in his treatment of the sanctuary and Maccabeus, then left.

**13:24** He appointed Hegemonides as governor of the territory from Ptolemais to Gerra.

**13:25** He went to Ptolemais; the people of Ptolemais were incensed at the treaty, indignant over it, and wanted to annul its provisions.

**13:26** Lysias went up to the public platform, gave the best defense he could, won them over, mollified them, and secured their goodwill; then he returned to Antioch. Such was the outcome of the king's campaign and his retreat.
